articles.title: The Limit of Nature: Thucydides and the Politics of Theory
articles.abstract: This article reconsiders Thucydides’s role as a foundational theorist of human nature. Contrary to conventional readings, I argue that Thucydides approaches “nature” ( physis ) less as a universal principle of behavior than as a site of political and theoretical investigation. By distinguishing his authorial voice from those of his speakers, I demonstrate that his analysis consistently approaches human nature as a limit concept—a baseline and boundary of human capacity that emerges in moments of existential precarity—while introducing a more nuanced set of terms to describe the habitual behaviors of political groups. By nevertheless foregrounding the more robust and determinative concept of nature in moments of contentious deliberation, Thucydides encourages reflection on the political dynamics that generate essentialist theories in public discourse. His account thus serves as a helpful point of reference for thinking about how competitive, polarizing speech affects the substantive categories of political debate and analysis, and through them political action.

articles.title: How Sociotropic Aesthetic Judgments Drive Opposition to Dense Housing Development
articles.authors: DAVID E. BROOCKMAN, CHRISTOPHER S. ELMENDORF, JOSHUA L. KALLA
articles.abstract: Voter opposition to dense housing development contributes to America’s housing shortage. Prevailing explanations emphasize homeowner self-interest and “NIMBYism.” We develop a theory of how sociotropic aesthetic judgments shape housing policy preferences and demonstrate its unique implications with a series of descriptive studies and experiments. First, people who choose to live in dense neighborhoods have an aesthetic taste for density, leading homeowners in already-dense areas to be more supportive of dense development both in their neighborhoods and elsewhere. Second, voters are more supportive of dense development when it is proposed in already-dense neighborhoods where it “fits”—even voters who live in those same dense neighborhoods. Finally, genuine aesthetic distaste for tall buildings is widespread and causally affects support for development. Our findings offer a new lens for understanding housing policy preferences and suggest novel solutions for addressing America’s housing shortage.

articles.title: Rising Wages and the Decline of Low-Wage Work
articles.authors: Clem Aeppli, Soohyun Roh, Nathan Wilmers
articles.abstract: From 2014 to 2024, the share of U.S. hourly workers paid below $15 in real terms fell by two-thirds, from 38 percent to 13 percent. Why? We first distinguish the entry and exit of employers—wherein high-paying employers have supplanted low-paying ones—from organizational changes among incumbent employers. Organizational changes can be imposed on employers by external constraints, like labor market tightness, or emerge from the pursuit of new opportunities. Using panel data drawn from administrative records and job reviews, we bring this framework to bear on the recent wage gains at the bottom of the labor market. Contrary to predictions of creative destruction, we can trace only a small amount of these wage gains to the disappearance of low-wage organizations. Instead, the main driver of rising pay was low- and middle-paying incumbent employers of low-wage occupations increasing pay. These gains in low-wage occupations were associated with tightening labor markets and increased minimum wages. But over and above these external constraints, employers also pursued new opportunities for reorganizing work in low-skill jobs. Notwithstanding organizational inertia, major gains for workers’ pay can come from changes in existing workplaces.

articles.title: From Wealth to Welfare: How Economic Elites Made Inequality Work
articles.abstract: Why do advanced economies engage in substantial income transfers but scarcely redistribute wealth? This paper argues that wealth inequality historically led economic elites to expand income transfers to propertyless households to stabilize the unequal property order. I study this proposition in the context of landholding inequality in Prussia. Estate owners, I argue, used income transfers to offset the economic insecurities of landless workers who could not rely on landownership as insurance against income loss. I digitize surveys of local poor relief and exploit Prussia’s administrative structure, where estates functioned as independent local authorities. The results show that landholding inequality caused higher income transfers to the poor, driven by the redistributive actions of estate owners. Estate owners allocated relief as social protection over the life cycle for households outside of the active workforce. This commitment to insurance was associated with greater voter support for the conservative parties representing estate owners’ interests.

articles.title: Challenging the Secular State: Faith-Based Drug Rehabilitation on the Rise in Brazil
articles.abstract: A significant achievement of Brazil’s evangelical Christian movement has been to secure public financing for religious drug rehabilitation. “Therapeutic communities” challenge the state’s longstanding commitment to a secular and scientifically-based public health system, which offers a credible alternative for drug treatment. That faith-based centers expanded under Workers’ Party presidents, which had historically defended Brazil’s estado laico and public healthcare system, is puzzling. The policy process literature helps explain this seeming paradox: rising illegal drug use opened a window of opportunity for religiously motivated actors to frame the problem in moral terms, gain initial traction through participatory venues, and set off policy feedback effects. These processes unfolded in a modernizing society marked by inequality and insecurity, creating fertile ground for the sacred to disrupt the secular.

articles.title: Production Function Estimation With Factor‐Augmenting Technology: An Application to Markups
articles.abstract: I develop a new method for estimating production functions with labor‐augmenting technology and apply it to markup estimation. The method imposes limited parametric restrictions and generalizes prior approaches that rely on the CES production function. I first extend the canonical Olley–Pakes framework assumptions to multidimensional productivity and then develop an identification strategy based on a control variable approach and first‐order conditions. I use this method to estimate output elasticities and markups in manufacturing industries in the US and four developing countries. I find that neglecting labor‐augmenting productivity underestimates capital elasticity, overestimates variable input elasticity, and overestimates markups in all countries.

articles.title: Intermediate Input Substitutability
articles.abstract: We estimate long‐run elasticities of substitution between intermediate inputs for Indian manufacturing plants. India's trade liberalization in the early 1990s provides an ideal natural policy experiment, with permanent and heterogeneous tariff reductions inducing changes in relative prices which we use for identification. We find a high degree of substitutability at the plant‐level between 8 broad categories of material inputs, significantly above the Cobb–Douglas benchmark of 1. In contrast, when considering shorter time horizons or more transitory shocks to relative prices, we find evidence of much lower elasticities. Using our long‐run elasticities in a quantitative model, we find that misallocation of intermediate inputs causes a reduction in aggregate output of 29%–3.5 times larger relative to a standard calibration with complementary inputs.

articles.title: Comment on ‘Selection and Comparative Advantage in Technology Adoption’ by Tavneet Suri
articles.authors: Emilia Tjernström, Dalia Ghanem, Aleksandr Michuda, Oscar Barriga-Cabanillas, Travis J. Lybbert, Jeffrey D. Michler
articles.abstract: This paper illustrates and addresses weak identification in the correlated random coefficient (CRC) model that Suri (2011) uses to study agricultural technology adoption. Using the publicly available data set, which differs slightly from the version used in Suri (2011), we obtain different point estimates for the paper's main CRC model. To understand why these differences are as large as they are, we recast the CRC model as a more general random coefficient model in which the returns to hybrid adoption are restricted to be linear in comparative advantage. This reveals that the key structural parameter in the CRC model ( ϕ ), which governs the relationship between baseline productivity and the returns to adoption, is prone to a weak‐identification problem. We then propose a procedure to conduct weak‐identification robust inference on ϕ using test inversion. Our weak‐identification robust confidence intervals contain the original Suri (2011) point estimates, which suggests that the difference in results may be attributable to a combination of minor data differences and weak identification.

articles.title: Informal Redistribution Through Work
articles.abstract: We investigate work as informal redistribution, leveraging field experiments and firm‐level survey data from Kampala, Uganda. Employers and workers consistently choose redistribution through work over cash transfers, revealing a willingness to pay for work. By randomizing work tasks—some designed to have zero marginal product—we find that production value does not explain these choices: employers pay for zero‐value work. These patterns are also inconsistent with other relational benefits, such as social image concerns or networking. Instead, motivations are normative. Experimental evidence reveals an internalized norm for redistribution through work rooted in incentive arguments on the demand side—as employers stop requiring work only when workers have verifiable emergencies—and in reciprocity and dignity from earning on the supply side. The norm shapes both the organization and measurement of production: failing to account for redistribution through work makes firms appear significantly larger and less productive than they are.

articles.title: Extreme Value Theory With Heterogeneous Agents
articles.abstract: Extreme value processes feature in any economic model in which agents receive a number of draws from some distribution of values and we examine the behavior of the maximum value in the limit as the number of draws becomes large. This paper asks: Do the average outcomes of such processes change when different agents receive a different number of draws? To answer this, we allow the number of draws an agent receives from the underlying distribution of values (e.g., productivities, ideas, or utility shocks) to be given by a search technology , which reflects heterogeneity in the expected number of draws across different types of agents. We derive a new class of extreme value distributions that generalizes the three standard distributions (Fréchet, Gumbel, Weibull) by incorporating heterogeneity across agents. We generalize a result from Gabaix, Laibson, Li, Li, Resnick, and de Vries (2016) regarding extreme value outcomes and consider applications to aggregate productivity, markups, and social networks.

articles.title: Two‐Sided Markets Shaped by Platform‐Guided Search
articles.abstract: This paper investigates concerns that vertically integrated platforms like Amazon steer demand toward their own offers via algorithmic prominence, potentially harming consumers. On Amazon, for each product, the Buybox prominence algorithm selects one seller to feature, influencing which offers consumers consider. Using novel Amazon sales and Buybox (prominence) data, we estimate a structural model capturing the effects of such algorithmic prominence on consumer choices, seller pricing, and entry. We find that the platform can indeed steer demand as 95% of consumers consider only the Buybox offer. The Buybox is highly price‐elastic (−21), but skews toward Amazon's own offers, which are featured as frequently as observably similar offers priced 5% cheaper. Still, as consumers prefer these offers, this skew does not amount to self‐preferencing in the sense of harming consumers: consumer surplus is roughly maximized at the estimated Amazon Buybox advantage, which balances higher prices against showing consumers their preferred offers.

articles.title: An Exact t ‐Test
articles.abstract: Multivariate linear regression and randomization‐based inference are two essential methods in statistics and econometrics. Nevertheless, the problem of producing a randomized test for the value of a single regression coefficient that is exactly valid when errors are exchangeable, and which is asymptotically valid for the best linear predictor, has remained elusive. In this paper, we produce a test that is exactly valid with exchangeable errors and which allows for general covariate designs; covariates may be continuous as well as discrete and may be correlated. The test is asymptotically valid when the errors are not exchangeable, in particular in the presence of conditional heteroskedasticity.

articles.title: From Predictive Algorithms to the Automatic Generation of Anomalies
articles.abstract: How can we extract theoretical insights from machine learning algorithms? We take a familiar lesson: researchers often turn intuition into theoretical insight by constructing “anomalies”—specific examples highlighting hypothesized flaws in a theory, such as the Allais paradox. We develop procedures that replace researchers' intuitions with predictive algorithms: given a predictive algorithm and a theory, our procedures automatically generate anomalies for that theory. We illustrate our procedures by generating anomalies for expected utility theory. Based on a neural network that accurately predicts lottery choices, we recover known anomalies for expected utility theory and discover novel ones. In incentivized experiments, subjects violate expected utility theory on these algorithmically generated anomalies at rates similar to the Allais paradox and common ratio effect.

articles.title: Why Are the Wealthiest so Wealthy? New Longitudinal Empirical Evidence and Implications for Theories of Wealth Inequality
articles.authors: Joachim Hubmer, Elin Halvorsen, Sergio Salgado, Serdar Ozkan
articles.abstract: We study the lifecycle dynamics of wealth inequality using 1993–2019 Norwegian administrative panel data on wealth and income. Employing a novel budget‐constraint approach, we decompose the excess wealth of the top 0.1% households relative to the median between ages 45 and 64 into higher saving rates (36%), inheritances (31%), returns (28%), and labor income (5%). One‐quarter of the wealthiest—the “New Money”—start with negative wealth on average but accumulate rapidly through high labor income and exceptionally high saving rates and returns. The “Old Money” inherit substantial wealth and grow it through above‐average though more modest saving and returns. We use these dynamic facts to evaluate five standard wealth inequality models. Although these models match cross‐sectional wealth concentration, they fail to reproduce the distinct dynamics of New and Old Money. A heterogeneous entrepreneurship model with decreasing returns to scale technology and nonhomothetic preferences is consistent with the observed dynamics.

articles.title: Coalitions in Repeated Games
articles.abstract: This paper proposes a framework and solution concept for repeated coalitional behavior. We model history‐dependent schemes that use continuation promises and punishments to deter coalitions from blocking. We evaluate the effectiveness of these schemes with and without transferable utility, and apply the framework to study the implications of wage transparency in labor markets.

articles.title: Putting the ‘Finance’ Into ‘Public Finance’: A Theory of Capital Gains Taxation
articles.authors: Mark Aguiar, Benjamin Moll, Florian Scheuer
articles.abstract: Standard optimal capital tax theory abstracts from modeling asset prices, making it unsuitable for thinking about capital gains and wealth taxation. We study optimal redistributive taxation in an environment with asset‐price movements, adopting the modern finance view that asset prices fluctuate not only because of changing cash flows, but also due to other factors (“discount rates”). We show that a combination of realization‐based capital gains and cash flow taxes implements the optimal allocation regardless of the source of asset‐price fluctuations. Moreover, the capital gains tax avoids distortions in portfolio choice (the so‐called lock‐in effect) by targeting total net trades rather than gains from selling individual assets. These results stand in contrast to the classic Haig–Simons comprehensive income tax concept as well as recent proposals for wealth or accrual‐based capital gains taxes.

articles.title: Optimal Formula Instruments
articles.abstract: When estimating the effects of treatments defined by complex formulas, researchers often use simple functions of exogenous shocks as instruments. A leading example is “simulated instruments” for public policy eligibility, which capture variation in state‐level policy generosity. We show how more powerful instruments can be constructed by incorporating heterogeneous shock exposure while using a recentering procedure to avoid bias. We characterize the asymptotically efficient instruments in this class and propose an algorithm for constructing feasible approximations to them. Compared to a simulated instrument approach, our approach yields a 44% smaller standard error on the private insurance crowd‐out effect of Medicaid enrollment from the 2014 Affordable Care Act expansions.

articles.title: The Social Learning Barrier
articles.abstract: Long‐lived agents interact repeatedly in a social network. In each period, each agent observes a private signal, chooses an action, and then observes the actions of her neighbors. We show that the learning rate of the slowest‐learning agent is capped by a constant that depends only on the distribution of the most informative private signal, but not on the number of agents, the network structure, correlations between the private signals, or the agents' strategies. For equilibrium learning with rational agents, the same result bounds the learning rate of every agent in any equilibrium under a broad class of conditions. The result is driven by an information‐theoretic tradeoff between optimal action choices and information revelation.

articles.title: Carbon emissions regulation, input-output networks, and firm dynamics: The case of a low-carbon-zone pilot in China
articles.abstract: Input-output linkages among sectors and firms are largely overlooked when assessing regulatory policies. Using a carbon emissions regulation in China as an example, we find that the regulation facilitates the transition to green technologies and reduces entry and carbon emissions in the regulated sectors with large carbon emissions. We also find unintended spillovers via the input-output network, resulting in more entry and innovation in the downstream sectors; and less entry and innovation in the upstream sectors. These facts can be rationalized by a firm-dynamics model with input-output linkages. The results of quantitative exercises are substantially different when taking input-output linkages into account.

articles.title: Enclaves and Assimilation in the Age of Mass Migration: Evidence from Ethnic Catholic Churches
articles.authors: Ran Abramitzky, Leah Boustan, Osea Giuntella
articles.abstract: Local ethnic amenities can foster the growth of immigrant enclaves, affecting economic and cultural integration. We study the centralized placement of “ethnic” Catholic churches in the United States during the Age of Mass Migration (1900-1930), focusing on Polish and Italian immigrants. Polish immigrants relied more heavily on the local parish to organise communal life. Following the opening of a Polish (but not Italian) church, co-ethnic residents experienced declines in occupation-based earnings but strengthened communal ties, measured by in-group marriage and naming, relative to matched neighbourhoods. These effects persist into the second generation and are not observed among other local residents, including Jews and non-Polish Catholics.

articles.title: Emotional State and Market Activity: Cause or Consequence?
articles.authors: Daniel Gotsman, Charles N Noussair, Yiwei Qu
articles.abstract: Many observers have asserted that there is a correlation between traders’ emotional states and asset market behaviour, with Joviality associated with high prices and Fear with low prices. In this paper, we conduct a laboratory experiment to examine the direction of causality in this relationship. The results show that moods, induced by videos, shown in virtual reality, do not influence market prices. However, there is a strong relationship between market activity and subsequent emotional states, suggesting that the correlation between emotional state and market activity is driven by the influence of market activity on emotional state, not the other way around.

articles.title: A mandate to multiply: the effects of pro-birth policies on fertility in colonial Congo
articles.abstract: Like other colonial powers, Belgium enacted pro-birth policies in its colony starting in the 1920s. We investigate their impacts on women who grew up in colonial Congo, using individual fertility outcomes for a sample of 30,000 women. Given that Catholic nuns implemented these policies, we exploit temporal and geographic heterogeneity in exposure to different types of missions, Catholic, Catholic with nuns and Protestants. We find that Catholic nuns succeeded in stimulating fertility, unlike other missionaries. We investigate mechanisms and show that Catholic female education – and its promotion of domesticity – played a decisive role. Finally, we find modest traces on fertility today.

articles.title: A Comparative Analysis of Refugee Policies in Southern Africa Refugee Reception in Southern Africa: National and Local Policies in Zambia and South Africa. By NicholasMaples, London, UK: University of London Press, 2024. ISBN: 978‐1‐90‐859076‐3
Migration Governance, Gender and the Identification of Trafficked Women: Evidence From Greece
articles.abstract: The early identification of trafficking victims is widely recognised as a key component of protection policies, yet little is known about how identification procedures operate in contexts shaped by restrictive migration governance. This article analyses the identification of women victims of trafficking in Greece between 2015 and 2019 through a gender‐sensitive and intersectional lens. Drawing on seventeen interviews with policy implementers and policy experts, together with field observations, it examines whether identification procedures reflected a victim‐centred approach and how EU and national migration policies shaped frontline practices. Findings show that identification often occurred within overcrowded and unsafe settings where the interaction between gender, nationality, migration status, socio‐economic resources and migration trajectories was insufficiently considered. Procedures relied heavily on victims' self‐reporting, while the hotspot framework, geographical restrictions and fragmented responsibilities hindered proactive detection. The article argues that these dynamics revealed a tension between formal commitments to early identification and the operational priorities of migration governance, limiting the implementation of gender‐sensitive identification mechanisms and contributing to forms of institutional invisibility for trafficked women within asylum and reception systems. These findings also provide a basis for assessing the subsequent development of formal identification mechanisms in Greece. In light of the new Pact on Migration and Asylum, the operational pressures identified in this study may remain relevant unless accelerated screening and border procedures are accompanied by effective vulnerability detection, referral mechanisms and protection safeguards.

articles.title: Softening the spring: Sensitization of transient media effects through repeated exposure over time
articles.authors: Yuqian Ni, Joshua Baldwin, Allan D Tate, Michael D Schmidt, Kyle Johnsen, Sun Joo (Grace) Ahn
articles.abstract: Existing longitudinal media effects research often emphasizes overall trends in behavioral or attitudinal changes, while overlooking fluctuations that occur before and after each exposure instance. This oversight can obscure the mechanisms underlying longitudinal media effects, particularly how they accumulate from successive short-term effects. We hypothesized a sensitization process where a single media exposure induces a transient change in behavior followed by a rapid decay, while repeated exposure gradually strengthen the magnitude of transient effects and make them more sustained. We tested this hypothesis by analyzing continuously recorded behavioral data collected via wearable sensors over 6 months. During this period, children repeatedly interacted with an integrated system of media technology designed to promote physical activity (PA). Data partially supported the hypothesized sensitization process. Children’s PA showed a transient increase following single exposures. Moreover, although the transient effect did not become more sustained over time, it grew in magnitude with repeated exposure.

articles.title: From Secular to Sectarian: How Political Secularism’s Decline Fuels Violence
articles.abstract: This article argues that contemporary religious violence arises largely from a global crisis of political secularism. Whereas much of the literature on the causes of religious violence emphasizes the conflict behavior of minority religious communities, we argue instead that religious violence stems centrally from empowered religious majorities , not from embattled religious minorities—a dynamic that has been exacerbated by the global secularism crisis. When states disproportionately discriminate against minority religious groups, they encourage extremists from favored groups to undertake violence. To test this theory, we employ a longitudinal statistical analysis of majoritarian religious violence across countries. The results reveal a robust positive association between government discrimination against religious minorities and majoritarian violence, consistent with our argument that the erosion of political secularism creates conditions conducive to religious violence.

articles.title: Strategic communication under constraint: using nonstate actor media to study relational dynamics in civil war
articles.authors: Emily K Gade, Shahryar Minhas, Bree Bang-Jensen, Kai Ping Leung, Michael Gabbay, Mohammed Hafez, Kayla Salehian, Ava Sharifi, Emily Kate Thomas, Arica Schuett, Tara Farkouh, Ramin Farrokhi, Willa Jeffers
articles.abstract: Between 2012 and 2018, Syrian rebel groups produced tens of thousands of social media posts documenting conflict events, alliances, and organizational identities. Although this media is propagandistic and not held to journalistic standards, it captures micro-level dynamics that conventional news sources often overlook, especially among smaller and lesser-known actors. In this article, we evaluate whether rebel-produced content can serve as a useful foundation for relational and locational observational conflict data. Drawing on roughly 28,000 social media posts, we construct the SAGAA (Syrian Armed Groups, Alliances, and Actions) dataset and leverage a latent variable network framework to compare the relational signal captured in SAGAA to that captured in the widely used UCDP Syria event dataset. We find that while SAGAA contains fewer total events, it captures a denser and less aggregated network of inter-rebel relationships—including ties absent from news sources but critical to understanding fragmented civil wars. These results are consistent with a theory of rebel self-reporting as strategic communication under constraint: armed groups have incentives to distort outcomes or minimize civilian harm, but face stronger credibility constraints when reporting jointly observable relational and locational details. Thus, we demonstrate the value of rebel media for recovering the relational structure and localized interactions that shape conflict dynamics, while underscoring the need for conflict-specific, triangulated approaches that complement rather than replace traditional news-based datasets.

articles.title: Political violence and waves of regime change
articles.abstract: A widely held view in conflict scholarship holds that nonviolent action is more successful than violent movements. This paper argues that a movement aiming at regime change that is part of a wave of similar movements is most likely to succeed if it relies on both violence and nonviolence. In a wave context, violence can remain a potential threat that affects subsequent movements, leading to domino effects that make outcomes in different countries interdependent. Observed levels of violence and nonviolence are thus a poor proxy for the real mechanisms of regime change. We develop a simple economic model of revolutionary overthrow of a regime and apply it to three waves of regime change: decolonization after World War II, the communist revolutions of 1917–1923, and the communist downfall of 1989–1991. Once the potential for violence is accounted for, coexistence of both techniques appears ubiquitous, often leading to the regime's disengagement. The failure of the communist revolution wave was due to the revolutionaries' misperception of past violence, driving them to insufficient resort to actual violence.

articles.title: Introducing UNGAInsight (1990–2023): new data on the United Nations General Assembly’s agenda
articles.authors: Bridget L Coggins, Jungjae Hong, Julia C Morse, Annjulie Vester
articles.abstract: Scholars use roll-call voting in the United Nations General Assembly to understand various political phenomena. Yet information on the politics of voting is limited because scholars lack details on the content and context of resolutions. This article fills this gap by providing new data: UNGAInsight (UNGA-I). UNGA-I complements existing datasets with new data on resolutions from 1990 to 2023, offering 32 mutually exclusive substantive topic categories that map onto the organization’s own committee-centered workflow. UNGA-I also includes information on which countries are targeted by specific resolutions and the nature of related demands. Finally, it provides more detailed information on the political dynamics that undergird absences. The data will allow researchers to develop more nuanced understandings of the UN and its political relevance across time. Additional insight into the UNGA’s agenda also raises questions about the common practice of using UN voting patterns as an indicator of alignment with the U.S.-led liberal international order.

articles.title: People know who to ask for favors despite underestimating compliance
articles.authors: Casher D. Belinda, Brittany C. Solomon
articles.abstract: Whether and how people approach social interactions hinges on how they expect others to respond. Extensive social psychology research suggests that people are inaccurate interpersonal perceivers, overestimating negative responses (e.g., discomfort) and underestimating positive responses (e.g., appreciation) across a variety of social situations. However, this conclusion is based almost exclusively on mean-level bias analyses that obscure the dyadic nature of interpersonal judgment and rely on a narrow conceptualization of interpersonal accuracy. Leveraging research on favor-asking and anticipated compliance as an exemplar, we demonstrate that interpersonal accuracy takes multiple theoretically distinct forms, and that the prevailing conclusion that people misunderstand their influence over others—because they tend to underestimate compliance—is likely overgeneralized. Across four studies (13,196 directed dyadic ratings), we show that people accurately differentiate between who will comply with their favor requests (dyadic meta-accuracy) despite the average tendency to underestimate compliance (mean-level bias). This pattern emerged for specific and general favor requests, among well- and newly-acquainted individuals, and beyond what could be expected due to self-projection. Through this dyadic lens, people are highly adept judges of their influence over others, as they are able to target their requests toward individuals who are uniquely likely to acquiesce to them—and can avoid wasting time on those who are not. Thus, our research refines existing implications for how people approach asking for favors. More broadly, by aligning theory, measurement, and level of analysis, our studies elucidate the need for greater theoretical precision and empirical breadth in interpersonal accuracy research.

articles.title: No evidence for a universal effect of writing on language use or the evolution of syntax
articles.authors: Carlo Y. Meloni, Jessica K. Ivani, Taras Zakharko, Guanghao You, Kellen Parker van Dam, Chundra A. Cathcart, Balthasar Bickel
articles.abstract: The acquisition of writing has a lasting effect on how languages are processed in the brain, raising the possibility that it also affects how they are used and evolve over time. A popular hypothesis is that writing specifically leads to the increased use and evolution of complex hierarchical structures in language. While most case studies on individual languages have supported this, it remains unclear whether results scale to larger and more diverse sets of languages. Here we test this prediction in two ways: 1) synchronically, by modeling the effect of modality (written vs. nonwritten) on syntactic complexity, operationalized via hierarchy depth and clause count inside sentences, in corpora from 30 languages; and 2) diachronically, by modeling whether the development of writing affected the phylogenetic dynamics of hierarchy in clause combinations across 59 languages from three families. We found no effect of writing on the response variables in either analysis. Hierarchy depth and clause count inside sentences do not demonstrably differ between spoken and written use of language, and the introduction of writing had no discernible effect on the evolution of clause combinations in grammar. There is weak evidence for a decrease in variance in structural asymmetry after the introduction of writing in one family, possibly reflecting the impact of increased normativity. Our findings challenge popular beliefs about the relationship between writing and hierarchy and suggest that the evolution of syntax is more driven by culturally variable ideas about style in linguistic expression than by the evolution of writing.

articles.title: Music illuminates sociocultural dimensions of autobiographical memory
articles.authors: Cara Turnbull, Benjamin M. Kubit, Kelly Jakubowski, Elizabeth H. Margulis
articles.abstract: Researchers have long theorized that autobiographical memory relies on sociocultural structures, such as life scripts and event schemas. The potency of music as a marker of social and personal identity, combined with its ubiquity in everyday life, allows us to connect these everyday scripts to larger patterns of socially and culturally shaped behavior. We collected free-response descriptions of autobiographical memories evoked by short clips of familiar songs from university undergraduates (n = 233). The songs spanned three popular genres and aligned with two significant periods of listeners’ lives. We analyzed the similarities and differences in the content of memories for particular songs using natural language processing. Memories cued by songs from the same category displayed striking similarities, suggesting that particular types of music cue memories that are similar between listeners but that vary according to characteristics such as music genre and release date. Two control conditions, in which a new set of participants reported memories evoked by key words from the lyrics (n = 121) and short narrative summaries of the lyrics (n = 129), indicate that these results cannot be explained by within-category similarities in the songs’ lyrical content. Instead, we suggest that the intersubjective structure of music-evoked autobiographical memories reflects socioculturally-defined scripts tied to song characteristics such as genre and release date. Thus, while memories may feel idiosyncratic and personal, there are also substantial similarities in life experiences between individuals with broadly similar backgrounds, and these shared experiences can be spontaneously called to mind through the seemingly innocuous act of turning on the radio.

articles.title: Stature reveals changing patterns of the biological standard of living in Europe and Asia over the past 7,000 y
articles.authors: Joerg Baten, Manon Stephan, Qiang Wang, Elizabeth Berger, John Brooke, Zhiwu Chen, Erdene Myagmar, Siân Halcrow, Kan Hou, Mark Hudson, Clark Spencer Larsen, Brian Padgett, Lanka Ranaweera, Charlotte Roberts, Noriko Seguchi, Richard H. Steckel, Xiaofan Sun, Naruphol Wangthongchaicharoen, Wanda Wang, Eun Jin Woo, Quanchao Zhang, Qun Zhang, Claudia Zancan, Qian Wang
articles.abstract: Human stature is a valuable indicator of nutritional status and health. Reconstructing this indicator allows insights into which types of societies were providing better health and nutrition—also termed the “biological standard of living” in the literature. Yet, archaeological evidence has not previously been assembled on a scale large enough for systematic comparison across premodern Eurasia. We present a dataset of 18,457 stature observations based on 783 sites from Asia and Europe, roughly spanning the 7,000 y before the twentieth century. Using harmonized estimates derived from long bones, we document broad regional variation in stature over time and examine how these patterns relate to population density and historical indicators of technological development. We observe marked declines in stature in most regions during the 500–1900 CE period, in both Asia and Europe. To interpret these patterns, we combine our stature series with estimates of population density, technological advancement, and related controls. As [Q. Ashraf, O. Galor, Am. Econ. Rev. 101 , 2003–2041 (2011)] predicted, higher technology levels were associated with higher population density, but not correlated with higher stature before the modern era. This relationship also holds after controlling for other potentially confounding factors such as latitude or transport access. By assembling the largest archaeological stature dataset for Eurasia to date and linking it to long-term demographic and historical indicators, this study provides an empirical basis for comparative research on premodern health, nutrition, and population pressure.

articles.title: Sustainability of violence prevention after a randomized vacant lot greening intervention in Philadelphia: A 10-y follow-up
articles.authors: Nicole Asa, Hiwot Y. Zewdie, Shadi Omidvar Tehrani, Maggie Beverly, Amy Carroll-Scott, Ali Rowhani-Rahbar, Andrew G. Rundle, Michelle C. Kondo, Jane E. Clougherty, Jessica Godwin, Charles C. Branas, Stephen J. Mooney
articles.abstract: Vacant lot greening has been shown to reduce violence and crime in the short-term [C. C. Branas et al. , Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. 115 , 2946–2951 (2018)]. We assessed the 10-y impact of a 2013 clustered randomized controlled trial (RCT) of lot greening in Philadelphia on violence and crime. We measured lot greening by treatment assignment from the original 2013 cluster RCT and a longitudinal greening score to assess the sustainability of the treatment assignment from 2012 through 2023. Our outcomes were the annual reported total crime, violent crime, and firearm violent crime per square mile at each lot. We conducted intent-to-treat and contamination-adjusted intent-to-treat analyses to estimate the local average treatment effect on relative change in crime. Lots randomized to the full greening intervention remained greener over time compared to other lots. In intent-to-treat analyses, compared to lots that received no intervention, lots that received any intervention had a 9% decrease in density of any crime (estimate = 0.91, 95%CI = 0.86, 0.96) and a 9% decrease in violent crime (estimate = 0.91, 95%CI = 0.86, 0.97) per square mile per year. In contamination-adjusted analyses, compared to lots without sustained greening treatment, lots with sustained greening treatment had a 12% decrease in density of any crime (estimate = 0.88, 95%CI = 0.83, 0.93) and an 11% decrease in density of violent crime (estimate = 0.89, 95%CI = 0.83, 0.95) per square mile per year. Even after a decade, vacant lot greening continues to prevent violence.

articles.title: Short-term flexibility and long-term stability in models of mind perception
articles.abstract: Understanding how people decide whether someone or something possesses a mind is central to a myriad of psychological, biological, and philosophical questions. It shapes fundamental processes at the individual (e.g., social interaction) and societal level (e.g., morality and ethics). While mind perception has been studied, it remains unclear which internal model people use when ascribing mental capacities to entities. Across four experiments (total N = 256), we explored what model people hold and its flexibility when ascribing agency and experience to entities encountered in everyday life and which differ in animacy and socialness (e.g., humans, pets, robots, voice assistants, tools). Using representational similarity analysis combined with lab-based experiments, a 6-wk long social interaction intervention, and longitudinal real-life exposure, we tested which model people use to ascribe agency and experience by comparing observed rating data to theoretical models. We demonstrated that an animacy distinction underlies the representational structure of experience attributions, while internal models for agency attributions are more idiosyncratic and flexible. When receiving explicit information on one entity, the internal model of agency changes. People update their model by incorporating this information, generalizing across the entire category of entities. We found no evidence that extended exposure to or ownership of inanimate technology, such as robots or voice assistants, or pets leads to restructuring of the models for experience or agency. Overall, these results provide insight into the internal models people hold when perceiving minds, the flexibility thereof, and offer ways to understand the roots and consequences of mind perception.

Coupled human–cattle mobility shaped the socioeconomic landscapes of the Holocene Middle Nile Valley
articles.authors: Marta Osypińska, Piotr Osypiński, Zdzislaw Belka, Louis Chaix, Patricia Anne Chiquet, Lionel Gourichon, Friederike Jesse, Olivier Langlois, Carlos Magnavita, Sonja Magnavita, Nadja Pöllath
articles.abstract: We present a synthesis of strontium isotope data ( 87 Sr/ 86 Sr) from human and cattle dental enamel across Middle Nile. This dataset, which combines newly acquired and published measurements, reveals a complex history of human and cattle mobility linked to ecological gradients and sociocultural changes in this part of the continent. During the early Holocene (8,000 to 4,000 BCE), isotopic unanimity in human and cattle remains supports early, correlated mobility of humans and Bos , extending beyond Nile floodplains to adjacent uplands. In the mid-Holocene (4,000 to 1,000 BCE), isotopic data from Wadi Howar suggest bidirectional corridors for mobility of both species linking the Middle Nile and the Western Desert. This pattern correlates with the emergence of the Middle Nile civilizations in which cattle played a central cultural and economic role. From the first millennium BCE onward, a radical change can be observed, correlated with the progressive desertification processes in the Sahel. Although cattle import routes continued to follow wadi systems, they shifted south of the now desiccated Saharan lakes toward Kordofan. The long-term perspective emphasizes the continuous adaptation of societies in the Middle Nile of what is now Sudan and adjacent regions to environmental changes, aimed at maintaining sustained access to cattle, a resource that remained crucial for Middle Nile communities throughout the Holocene.

articles.title: The debt burden of tropical cyclones and climate change
articles.authors: June Choi, Renzhi Jing, Christopher W. Callahan, Marshall Burke, Noah S. Diffenbaugh
articles.abstract: Addressing climate change through mitigation and adaptation is expected to require more than $6 trillion in global investment annually by 2035. Yet many countries face significant barriers to accessing this finance, including low or absent credit ratings, large debt burdens, and high borrowing costs. Climate change may further amplify these barriers, creating a “vicious cycle” in which mounting economic losses reduce the capacity of countries to invest in adaptation and mitigation. We provide evidence that the cost and availability of capital for many countries have already been shaped by both historical exposure to naturally-occurring tropical cyclones (TCs) and anthropogenic warming. Our empirical estimates suggest that, on average across TC-exposed countries, 20% of debt-to-GDP ratios are attributable to TCs from 1980 to 2019. Across all countries, GDP levels are on average 12% lower due to the combined impacts of baseline naturally-occurring TCs and anthropogenic warming. In a separate correlational machine-learning analysis, we estimate that these macroeconomic impacts are associated with an increased likelihood of hotter countries receiving credit ratings below investment grade ( < BBB–), as well as persistent credit risk premiums of at least 1 basis point in 64 countries and 5 basis points in highly exposed countries. We provide estimates for 181 countries, including many TC-affected and/or hot countries that do not have bond yield data. Future increases in temperature and TC activity may further worsen sovereign credit conditions, potentially undermining climate resilience and long-run development prospects.

articles.title: The sound of persuasion: Using generative AI to identify gender gaps in political influence
articles.authors: Ethan C. Busby, Lisa P. Argyle, Parker Davis, Joshua R. Gubler, Bryce Hepner, Christopher F. Karpowitz, Alex Lyman, Justin Olcott, Jessica R. Preece, David Wingate
articles.abstract: Women often experience a deficit in persuasive influence, particularly in contexts like politics, where expectations about women’s behavior may conflict with gendered expectations about the domain and role. In spite of this widespread pattern, the mechanisms behind the gender gap in persuasion are difficult to isolate and test in dynamic political conversations. Women may be less persuasive simply because role-based expectations prompt others to afford women less authority when speaking about politics generally or about some political topics. Alternatively, women may be less persuasive because they tend to use linguistic patterns or rhetorical strategies that are less effective. Using an original AI-based approach, we put 4,300 human subjects into realistic, real-time phone conversations with an AI agent. These agents were randomly assigned either a masculine or feminine gendered conversation topic and a male- or female-sounding voice, allowing us to manipulate topic and perceptions of speakers’ gender while holding constant other elements of rhetorical content and strategy. After validating the experimental treatments, we find no direct effects of perceived gender of the AI agent, as cued by voice. However, gender affects other important aspects of the persuasive interaction. Research subjects were more likely to be persuaded about the masculine topic (defense spending) than the feminine topic (aid to the poor). Additionally, women research subjects were, on average, more persuaded than men. To the extent that men and women emphasize different topics in political conversations and have different discussion partners, these dynamics are likely to shape women’s political persuasive influence.

articles.title: Morally motivated crimes are less sensitive to punishment
articles.abstract: Modern western legal and criminal justice theories assume that punishment should deter criminalized behavior by introducing costs that reduce its expected utility, but, empirically, punishment often has weak effects on rates of crime and recidivism. Here, we hypothesize that when people are motivated to engage in criminalized behavior for moral reasons, they show diminished sensitivity to punishment. We demonstrate our hypothesis across 10 correlational, experimental, and economic game studies with participants drawn from the general population as well as participants with criminal backgrounds. Studies 1 to 3 draw on federal data of over 30,000 offenders and find that participants’ estimates of moral motives for crime predict higher recidivism while estimates of material motives predict the opposite. Studies 4 to 8 use judgment studies and find that morally motivated crimes are less sensitive to punishment across a diversity of crime types, when motives are manipulated but actions are kept constant, persist for different types of consequences, and are unique to moral motivation. Studies 9 and 10 employ economic games and find that when players take money from others for moral reasons, they are less deterred by the imposition of fines. Implications for systems of punishment, offender psychology, and restorative justice approaches are discussed.

What Role Did Immigration Attitudes Play in Latinos’ 2016–2024 Swing Toward the GOP?
articles.abstract: After the 2012 and 2016 presidential elections, scholars and observers frequently characterized Latino voters as unlikely to support anti-immigration candidates, especially when immigration is salient. However, between 2016 and 2024, Latinos were among the groups that swung the most toward the GOP. Given the mismatch between Donald Trump’s strident opposition to unauthorized immigration and Latinos’ historically pro-immigration views, understanding the role of Latinos’ immigration attitudes in vote choice over this period is theoretically important. Acknowledging that Latinos are not single-issue voters, we investigate this question using multiple high-quality, population-based panels of Latinos (2016–2024). We document a sharp restrictionist turn in Latinos’ attitudes. We also find that Latinos perceive Democrats to have moderated slightly on immigration, though not enough to keep pace with the change in public opinion. Finally, we demonstrate that Latinos placed just as much weight on immigration policy in their 2024 vote choice as in 2016. Our results suggest that while immigration has not waned in importance for Latinos, changes in attitudes from 2016 to 2024 diminished Democrats’ advantage on this issue.

articles.title: Earnings Instability
articles.authors: Peter Ganong, Pascal Noel, Christina Patterson, Joseph Vavra, Alexander Weinberg
articles.abstract: This paper uses high-frequency administrative data to show that most U.S. workers experience substantial month-to-month fluctuations in pay, even within ongoing employment relationships. Monthly earnings instability is pervasive but is masked in annual data. Moreover, this instability is unequally distributed: lower-income, hourly workers face more instability than higher-income, salaried workers. Firm-driven fluctuations in hours account for a large share of this instability. Monthly earnings instability, in turn, increases spending volatility and job separations. Short-term earnings risk is therefore a significant feature of the labor market and falls disproportionately on the most financially fragile workers.

articles.title: Meritocracy and Homophily in Collegial Organizations
articles.abstract: In collegial organizations, homophily jeopardizes the recruitment of the most talented (“meritocracy”). We analyze the dynamics and welfare properties of an organization whose incumbent members coopt new ones in a forward-looking manner. We identify organizations in which meritocracy is likely to give way to favoritism and entrenchment, and investigate policy interventions (such as affirmative action, quality-based or diversity-based funding, discretionary overruling of majority decisions, blind hiring processes) and their unintended consequences.

articles.title: The Impact of Commercial Real Estate Regulations on U.S. Output
articles.authors: Fil Babalievsky, Kyle F Herkenhoff, Lee E Ohanian, Edward C Prescott
articles.abstract: Commercial real estate accounts for about 20% of the U.S. capital stock and is highly regulated. Yet relatively little is known about how these regulations affect economic activity or consumer welfare. This paper develops a spatial general equilibrium model of the U.S. economy with commercial real estate regulations and congestion effects, the latter providing a rationale for such regulations. The model constructs a panel of commercial real estate regulation indices for major U.S. metropolitan areas by exploiting variation in the share of parcel value attributable to land versus structures in tax assessor records compiled by Cotality. We find that a moderate relaxation of commercial real estate building regulations across U.S. cities generates large allocative efficiency gains, increasing output by 2.7% to 5.3% and welfare by 2.8% to 8.0% of lifetime consumption. We then extract the component of our regulatory indices that covaries with specific zoning attributes in LightBox data, including zoning height limits, and use it to simulate local deregulation policies. Relaxing height limits in New York City raises its output by 2.9%.

articles.title: Aspiring to a Better Future: Can a Simple Psychological Intervention Reduce Poverty?
articles.authors: Kate Orkin, Robert Garlick, Mahreen Mahmud, Richard Sedlmayr, Johannes Haushofer, Stefan Dercon
articles.abstract: Do higher aspirations for the future motivate people living in poverty to make long-term investments? Do their aspirations increase when economic conditions improve? To answer these questions, we run a 415-village field experiment with 8,300 women living in poverty in rural Kenya. We design an 80-minute workshop to help people set higher aspirations and plan to achieve them. We cross-randomise this with large unconditional cash transfers. The workshop substantially raises aspirations, labour supply, investment, revenue, and living standards 17 months later, relative to a placebo workshop. Increases in aspirations are the most likely mechanism to explain the economic effects. Cash transfers also raise aspirations, which might help to explain why transfers increase labour supply and investment. We conclude that aspirations respond to both economic and psychological interventions, contribute to investment decisions and living standards, and are important considerations for development policy.

articles.title: Daddy’s Girl: Daughters, Managerial Decisions, and Gender Inequality
articles.abstract: Using Danish registry data, we study how managers’ gender attitudes shape gender inequality in the workplace by exploiting the birth of a daughter—as opposed to a son—as a plausibly exogenous shock to male managers’ gender attitudes. Comparing within-firm changes in women’s labour outcomes depending on the gender of the manager’s newborn child, we find that women’s relative earnings and employment increase by 4.4% and 2.9%, respectively, following the birth of the manager’s first daughter. These effects are driven by an increase in managers’ propensity to substitute male hires with female hires that have comparable education, hours worked, and earnings. Consistent with this substitution channel, we do not detect any significant effect on firm performance. Because these effects emerge rapidly and persist over time, we can rule out the need for prolonged exposure to gender issues or for personal incentives tied to improving conditions for their own daughters as prerequisites for managers to promote gender equality within their firms.

articles.title: From Design to Disclosure
articles.authors: S Nageeb Ali, Andreas Kleiner, Kun Zhang
articles.abstract: We study the role of hard information in contractual and market settings in which the receiver can flexibly adjust allocations and transfers in response to the sender's disclosure. These settings include monopoly pricing, insurance contracting, and policy negotiations. Across these settings, the sender is worst off if she reveals her type completely because the receiver would then adjust the terms of trade to extract her surplus. Taking this feature as our central departure from the literature, we characterize the entire set of equilibrium payoffs in these disclosure games. We prove an equivalence result: a payoff profile can be approximated by an equilibrium of the disclosure game if and only if it can be achieved through information design. Thus, there exist equilibria in which the sender obtains approximately her commitment payoff.

articles.title: New Latinx destinations, adolescent friendship, and substance use: how migrant expansion inspires network revitalization
articles.abstract: Contrary to political rhetoric and stereotypes perpetuated by the media, Latinx migrants report lower rates of substance use than their native-born counterparts. These unanticipated benefits are not limited to migrants themselves but also strengthen the neighborhoods where they settle. Although social networks are frequently cited as a mechanism that could explain these patterns, it is unclear whether Latinx migrant expansion restructures our social networks. The current study addresses these gaps by offering the concept of network revitalization to describe how influxes of Latinx residents can reshape and reorient patterns of interaction. I evaluate the extent to which this social process occurs by applying stochastic actor-oriented models to fifty-three longitudinal adolescent friendship networks from rural Midwestern communities. Focusing on the coevolution of youth friendship and substance use, I compare the structural dynamics of networks embedded in new Latinx destinations to those in communities without growing Latinx populations. Results indicate that adolescents who use substances are less popular, less social, and less likely to form homogenous friendships when they attend school in new Latinx destinations versus non-destinations, though variations emerge across different substances. These findings suggest that network revitalization is an overlooked meso-level process that can help explain why migrant expansion enhances community well-being.

Class diplomacy: cross-class friendship, social mobility, and the promise of symbolic exchange
articles.abstract: Economists in the United States and UK have recently suggested that cross-class friendships are widespread and provide an important source of social capital for people from working-class backgrounds. However, these findings sit in tension with a broader sociological literature indicating that friendships rest on principles of reciprocity and equality and that cross-class friendships are rarely successful. In this paper, we interrogate this tension by drawing on forty-two in-depth interviews with people in cross-class friendships in the UK. Our findings indicate that while friendships formed across class can produce social capital for those from less advantaged backgrounds, such one-way transfers often generate feelings of inequality or indebtedness. In some instances, this is a source of ongoing tension or downward spirals in friendships. However, in successful cross-class friendships, we find that class difference is negotiated via a process we term “class diplomacy.” We outline three modes of class diplomacy: (1) joking—using humor to recognize and defuse class tensions; (2) avoiding—prioritizing emotional intimacy over discussions of class to protect the friendship; and (3) confronting—openly discussing class differences to build empathy and shared understanding. Our findings suggest that, when enacted successfully, class diplomacy can pave the way for forms of symbolic exchange to develop between friends, which both has a mutual socializing effect and can lead to a heightened political sensitivity to class inequality.

articles.abstract: This paper offers an explanation of the disparate concern Westerners have for civilians who die in different wars abroad. I consider two attempts to explain the disparate concern in terms of racism: first a more interpersonal understanding of racism as racist animus, and then a more structural explanation in terms of “white ignorance.” I argue that trying to understand the disparate concern evinced for different civilian casualties primarily in terms of racism is mistaken, and that a Marxist account of imperialism offers a plausible framework for explaining Western attitudes. The paper also argues for the interplay between imperialism and race, and for the philosophical importance of considering the role of imperialism and capitalism when considering race, racism, and white ignorance.

articles.title: Off the Record? Effects of Interview Audio Recordings on Interviewer Behavior
articles.authors: Lukas Olbrich, Jonas Beste, Joseph W Sakshaug, Silvia Schwanhäuser
articles.abstract: Survey interviewers are usually instructed to follow standardized interviewing procedures when conducting interviews. The introduction of computer-assisted interviewing facilitated the collection of interview audio recordings to assess if interviewers indeed follow these standardized procedures. However, in most cases, audio recordings require respondent consent, and thus interviewers know whether an interview is recorded or not. In this paper, we analyze the extent to which interviewers change their behavior when interviews are recorded. Using automatically collected timestamp data and both cross-sectional and longitudinal analysis approaches to account for selection effects, we find that interviewers substantially change their behavior when recorded. Our results show that audio recordings lead to substantially fewer very short and very long questionnaire module durations and increase the average time spent on questionnaire modules, which is in line with a deterrence effect. Concerning substantive outcomes, we find larger interviewer effects for estimates derived from non-recorded than for recorded interviews.

articles.title: DNA, Self-reported Ancestry, and Social Scientific Inquiry
articles.abstract: Highlights All humans share one vast family tree, and our place in it leaves a partial imprint on our DNA. Genetic similarity proportions estimate how closely one’s DNA resembles that of various reference groups. Our framework estimates genetic similarity while limiting bias from researchers’ cultural schemas. Within ancestry groups, genetic similarity varies widely and indexes racialized physical traits. Genetic data offer researchers a lens for studying, not disputing, the social construction of race.

articles.title: Disrupted Timing, Enduring Norms: Return Migration and Fertility in Argentina, Romania, Senegal, and Ukraine
articles.authors: Inmaculada Serrano, Héctor Cebolla‐Boado, Teresa Castro‐Martín
articles.abstract: Return migration remains understudied in the migration–fertility literature, despite returnees accounting for up to 25 percent of all international movements. This article examines whether the fertility patterns of return migrants—a highly mobile population experiencing at least two moves: migration and return—resemble or diverge from those of nonmigrants in their countries of origin. Using a unique cross‐country dataset encompassing four diverse socioeconomic and migration contexts (Argentina, Romania, Senegal, and Ukraine), we examine three key fertility outcomes: timing of first birth, completed fertility, and childlessness. Our findings reveal a general pattern of similarity between returnees and nonmigrants across nearly all contexts. A singular exception is that the transition to the first child is significantly delayed during the migration period. However, our evidence demonstrates that this disruption is largely a temporal effect, as a robust recuperation effect is observed upon return. Furthermore, although large and statistically significant delays occur during migration among women in Ukraine and men in Argentina and Senegal, these do not necessarily translate into a permanent reduction in family size. Specifically, return migrants in most groups register completed fertility similar to those of nonmigrants.

articles.title: Commonalities and Differences in Lowest‐Low Fertility Patterns
articles.abstract: Lowest‐low fertility has been extensively studied, particularly in the Global North. Much less is known about whether these patterns will repeat across other regions of the world. As demographic theories evolve to explain recent trends, there is a growing need to understand how emerging patterns of fertility decline in the Global South might be (dis)similar to past trends observed in the Global North. Using an empirical approach, we examine 34 countries that experienced a period total fertility rate (TFRp) ≤ 1.3 for at least one year between 1950 and 2023, with the aim of identifying common patterns and possible trajectories. The findings reveal heterogeneous yet comparable dynamics: after initially spreading at the end of the 20th century, the diffusion of lowest‐low fertility appeared to stall. However, since the early 2010s, the number of countries with TFRp ≤ 1.3 has increased, affecting both more and less developed countries. Our cohort analysis suggests that additional countries may soon join this group. We argue that lowest‐low fertility results from the combination of declining early fertility and the absence of compensatory increases in late fertility. These processes should be examined starting from different theoretical explanations, with attention to differences between more and less developed countries.

Policy Design and Polarization: How Policy Characteristics Moderate the Relationship Between Issue and Social Polarization
articles.authors: Johnathan Noah Wolff, Deven E. Carlson, Adam Tyner
articles.abstract: Political scientists distinguish between issue‐based polarization (i.e., partisan differences in policy preferences) and identity‐based polarization (i.e., social animus between individuals with different identities, political or otherwise) and have shown that the latter can drive increases in the former. We extend this work by exploring whether policy characteristics moderate the extent to which identity‐based polarization leads to issue polarization. We draw on prior research to identify seven policy characteristics across three broad categories (policy uncertainty, policy breadth, and policy familiarity) that, when combined, shape the likelihood of identity‐based polarization driving issue polarization around the policy. Our empirical assessment of this proposition draws on data from two separate surveys that polled respondents about their views on three different education policy topics: Social and Emotional Learning, Critical Race Theory, and affirmative action. Consistent with our expectations, results across each of the three policy areas show that identity‐based gaps in support for policies that exhibit these characteristics are substantially larger than support gaps around policies where these characteristics are absent.

articles.title: (No) Longer Dependent: The Link between Reception, Housing, and Civic Integration Policies and Social Assistance Dependency among Refugees in the Netherlands
articles.abstract: We analyzed how key aspects of refugees’ reception and civic integration experiences relate to their probability of exiting social assistance for employment in the Netherlands. We focused on the duration of stay in reception centers, relocations between centers, completion of the civic integration program, and the language level of the integration diploma. We used administrative data on approximately 95,000 refugees who received refugee residence permits between 2014 and 2022. We conducted robustness analyses using a cohort of approximately 21,000 Syrian refugees who received residence permits between 2014 and 2016 and representative survey data on 2,553 members of this cohort, which allowed us to control for pre-migration education and employment. Multilevel linear probability discrete-time survival models showed distinct gender patterns. Among men, the monthly hazard of exiting social assistance increased until approximately 3 years after housing and subsequently declined, whereas among women it increased gradually throughout the observation period. Prolonged stays in reception centers were associated with a lower hazard of employment among men, particularly among those who stayed for more than 2 years, and this disadvantage persisted over time. Among women, the differences by reception duration were small and inconsistent. Relocations had a small and temporary association with employment. Completing civic integration was strongly associated with labor market entry for men and women, and these differences remained substantial 5 to 6 years after housing. B1- and B2-level integration diplomas were generally associated with a higher probability of exiting social assistance than A2-level diplomas.
