articles.title: Scarcity in crises: access disparities to COVID-19 vaccines among natives, migrants, and refugees in Germany
articles.abstract: This paper investigates disparities in the timing of COVID-19 vaccination uptake among natives, migrants, and refugees in Germany. Using data from the representative, nationwide RKI-SOEP-2 survey and employing Kaplan–Meier survival analysis, Cox proportional hazard models, and an Oaxaca–Blinder decomposition, the study reveals a significant temporal gap and associated factors. Natives received their vaccination earlier than migrants, and those in turn earlier than refugees. While accounting for differences in eligibility and individual vaccination intentions, the paper examines the role of potential access barriers. In line with fundamental cause theory, key flexible resources such as income, language skills, social networks, and access to transportation are found to be significantly associated with vaccination timing. Differences in these flexible resources account for a substantial share of the observed gap in vaccination timing between natives, migrants, and refugees. The paper highlights how structural disadvantages can have direct public health implications. The results stress that—beyond the health crisis of the COVID-19 pandemic—ensuring fair access to scarce resources is essential to prevent existing social inequalities from translating into health disparities during crises.

articles.title: Does policy evaluation depend on the quality of democracy?
articles.abstract: Policy evaluation contributes to the quality of democracy, but does the quality of democracy, in turn, contribute to the production and use of policy evaluation? Existing research provides evidence for the former claim but not for the latter. Addressing this research gap, this article examines the pertinence of democratic characteristics alongside or in combination with economic, bureaucratic and educational capacities and analyses the extent to which they are necessary or sufficient for the production and use of policy evaluation. Drawing on Bertelsmann’s Sustainable Governance Indicators (SGI), the analysis applies fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) to all 41 OECD and EU countries. The results suggest that a strong balance of powers and access to information are necessary, but not sufficient conditions for the production and use of policy evaluation. Instead, democratic settings provide an enabling context that must be matched by strong bureaucratic and educational capacities for policy evaluation to be produced and used. Conversely, pathways involving weak democratic accountability, insufficient educational and economic capacities, or insufficient bureaucratic capacity, result in the absence of the production and use of policy evaluation. By shedding light on the tenuous relationship between policy evaluation and democracy, this article carries important implications for policy evaluation and evidence use in countries facing democratic decline and the political erosion of state capacities.

articles.title: The politics of policy transfer: political dynamics in OECD accession
articles.abstract: While recent scholarship has called for greater attention to the political dynamics of policy transfer, this dimension remains under-theorised in policy studies. Existing work has convincingly shown that transfer is politically motivated yet often lacks analytical tools capable of systematically unpacking these dynamics. This article examines the politics of policy transfer empirically. Drawing on political sociology, it conceptualises policy transfer as a process of mobilisation by interested actors occupying positions within organisational fields. These actors use policy transfer as an opportunity to mobilise resources and advance their positions, while seeking to legitimate their choices among national and transnational audiences. Building on three analytical dimensions – fields, opportunities, and legitimacy – the article examines policy transfer associated with the accession of Chile and Colombia to the OECD during the 2010s and 2020s. The analysis shows that transfer was driven, at the transnational level, by the OECD’s efforts to reinforce its relevance within the multilateral field, particularly in the Latin American region, while domestically it was shaped by governing elites seeking economic capital in the form of foreign investment and symbolic capital through international recognition. The article concludes by showing how attention to fields, opportunities, and legitimacy can advance understanding of the political dynamics that shape policy transfer.

articles.title: Explaining policy stasis on same-sex unions in Peru
articles.abstract: This article advances understanding of how policy monopolies sustain policy stasis in morality policy, where scholarship has explained policy change more fully than its absence. It develops the concept of a moral policy monopoly to examine how interlocking mechanisms can sustain policy stasis in contexts of high religiosity. Using abductive, mechanistic and analyticist process tracing, and drawing on documents and interviews, the study examines three decades of legislative inertia on same-sex unions in Peru, where 17 Bills were submitted to Congress between 1993 and 2024 and none advanced to plenary approval. The analysis identifies five interlocking mechanisms through which ultraconservative religious actors sustain stasis under conditions of high religiosity, substantial church capacity and a religiously embedded party system. Forging alliances, building moralised policy images and capturing politics operate continuously, while joint opposition campaigns and competing Bills operate episodically in response to triggering events. Each mechanism presupposes or reinforces the others, so stasis emerges from interlocking and deliberate activity rather than dispersed opposition. By showing how these mechanisms work together to prevent policy change, the article demonstrates how policy monopolies can actively sustain stasis in morality policy. These mechanisms also reveal religiosity not as a background condition but as a resource that actors convert into political capacity.

articles.title: Why policy actors choose not to coordinate in policy conflicts
articles.authors: Fredrik Johansson, Örjan Bodin, Daniel Nohrstedt
articles.abstract: Research on advocacy coalitions in public policy highlights the importance of coordination among policy actors seeking to influence policy making. Less attention has been devoted to why actors sometimes choose not to coordinate, even when they share similar beliefs or interests. In this study, we explore the rationales behind actors’ decisions to refrain from publicly visible coordination in wind power development projects in two Swedish municipalities over a 16-year period. Our findings show that, while most actors engage in coordination at some point, they also refrain from coordinating with others for several reasons. First, they perceive alternative means of exerting influence as more cost-effective; second, they have concerns about the trustworthiness of like-minded actors; third, they view the long-term consequences of coordination as uncertain; and fourth, they are less willing to coordinate when conflict is high, unless they represent political parties. These findings show that shared beliefs or interests do not necessarily translate into coordination and identify conditions that can constrain collective action among policy actors. The study contributes to research on advocacy coalitions by bringing decisions not to coordinate more explicitly into explanations of collective action in contested policy subsystems.

articles.title: Strategic Moralization in Parliamentary Debates
articles.authors: Minahil Malik, Hanna Bäck, Emma Baker, Royce Carroll, Robert Klemmensen
articles.abstract: Moralization, the framing of political conflict in terms of right and wrong rather than as pragmatic trade‐offs, is thought to both mobilize and persuade audiences, but may also make compromise less acceptable. This article examines when and why representatives employ moralizing rhetoric. We argue that moralizing rhetoric varies with the circumstances that shape the incentives representatives face. We examine whether such rhetoric is more common among opposition and outsider or niche parties and intensifies as elections approach. Because moralization in parliamentary rhetoric often operates through implicit framing rather than explicit moral vocabulary, we apply a generative large language model (LLM) with chain‐of‐thought prompting to Swedish parliamentary debates from 1991 to 2023. We find that moralization is substantially higher among nongoverning parties and increases before elections. Examining whether representatives from niche or outsider parties tend to moralize more, we find some evidence of higher moralization among the Left and Green parties, but not among the right‐wing populists when government status is accounted for.

articles.title: The Rise of Amateur Candidate Pipelines and Declining Value of Candidate Experience in U.S. Senate Primaries, 1980–2024
articles.authors: Carlos Algara, Byengseon Bae, Isaac Hale, Michael Heseltine, Evan Lieber
articles.abstract: Given the increasing nationalization of elections, research on U.S. electoral competition has shifted to emphasize same‐party competition rather than general elections. Much of this work, especially arguments that electoral amateurs are increasingly likely to win party nominations, focuses almost exclusively on U.S. House elections, leaving the more competitive U.S. Senate largely outside systematic inquiry. In this manuscript, we address this gap by introducing new data covering all candidates who filed to run for the U.S. Senate from 1980 to 2024, including primary contestants and candidates who later withdrew. We provide three descriptive findings. First, inexperienced candidates increasingly enter Senate primaries, especially Republican ones, while the number of experienced candidates remains stable. Second, congruent with the House, candidate quality declines as a predictor of primary success and is now statistically insignificant in both parties. Third, we rule out fundraising convergence and call for further research on mechanisms shaping the declining value of candidate experience.

articles.title: Gender and Presiding Roles in Legislatures: Discrepancies in Mass and Elite Perceptions From Parallel Survey Experiments
articles.authors: Yuya Endo, Hirofumi Miwa, Hikaru Nukui, Yoshikuni Ono
articles.abstract: Women are far less likely than men to serve as chairs of legislatures—a disparity often attributed to gender norms that associate leadership with men and assign women to subordinate roles. We test these assumptions about the gender gap in legislative leadership using vignette experiments with over 4000 voters and 7000 elected municipal council members in Japan. We find a significant gap between voters' perceptions of legislators' preferences and council members' evaluations of women's suitability for leadership. Voters believe council members prefer men as chairs and women as vice‐chairs, whereas council members view female colleagues as equally or more suitable for both roles. These results suggest that legislators' expressed gender bias alone may not fully explain women's underrepresentation as presiding officers and that institutional or supply‐side constraints may also play a role. By distinguishing voters' perceptions of elite preferences from elites' own evaluations, our micro‐level evidence contributes to debates over women's underrepresentation in political leadership.

articles.title: When Oversight Stops Producing Answers: Parliamentary Questions and Executive Accountability in Turkey
articles.abstract: Under what conditions does an oversight instrument remain formally available while ceasing to produce answers, and how does that loss unfold when measured directly rather than inferred from the rules? Where comparative research reads legislative constraint from the instruments a parliament possesses, this article reads it from what those instruments yield, using every question submitted to the Turkish Grand National Assembly between 1999 and 2026 and its record of when ministries answered. Under a durable single‐party majority, the share of written questions answered within the statutory period eroded gradually, then settled at a low floor; no political milestone produces a step in that trend. The later abolition of oral questions and the motion of censure aligned the rules with an amended constitution and left no detectable change in the surviving instrument. The decline reached the governing party's own questions and fell hardest on the DEM Party lineage. Oversight weakened in a particular order, yield first and gradually, formal availability last and abruptly; measures built from formal availability date that loss to the wrong moment.

articles.title: Partisan Delay: Gubernatorial Discretion and Representation in Special Elections
articles.abstract: How do governors work as partisan agents to influence legislative control and representation? This article examines a unique power given to governors to select the timing of congressional and state legislative special elections. We theorize that governors are active partisan agents who expedite and delay special election timing based on whether the vacancy will favor or disfavor their party. We test this using two novel datasets on special elections in the U.S. House from 1959 to 2024 and state legislatures from 2009 to 2024. We find that governors systematically delay special elections when the opposing party is expected to win, with effects more pronounced in the modern era. These findings have significant implications for representation, demonstrating that even safe districts can be deprived of representation due to partisan demands. We contribute to the burgeoning literature on election timing, demonstrating the role partisan actors play in shaping the election calendar.

Negotiating Competing Expectations—Chiefs and Mineral Governance in Ghana
articles.abstract: This paper examines what shapes chiefs' discretionary decision‐making and how they exercise authority within hybrid governance arrangements, focusing on Ghana's artisanal and small‐scale mining (ASM) sector. Existing scholarship recognizes that traditional authorities can strengthen or undermine state governance but offers limited explanations for variation in their practices. Drawing on interviews with chiefs, miners, and state officials, the paper develops a discretionary governance framework that integrates hybrid governance, access theory, and discretion. It argues that overlapping customary and statutory authority creates a discretionary space for chiefs to navigate competing expectations. Chiefs exercise this discretion through diverse governance practices, including restricting access to mining sites, mobilizing communities, and collaborating with state institutions, as well as facilitating access to land, negotiating informal payments, and shielding unauthorised miners from enforcement. These practices can reinforce, negotiate, circumvent, or undermine formal mining regulation. The paper advances debates on traditional authority and hybrid governance while challenging assumptions that constitutionally empowering chiefs necessarily strengthens mineral governance.

articles.title: “Unseen and unheard”: Recognition and Its Role in Shaping Administrative Burden
articles.abstract: Administrative burden scholarship has identified psychological costs alongside learning and compliance costs, yet the category remains homogeneous, grouping stigma, diminished autonomy, and stress, without a shared organizing principle. This article advances a mechanism-level account centered on recognition, drawing on a qualitative case study of claiming disability benefits in Israel, based on in-depth interviews with 33 individuals (16 young adults with diagnosed mental health conditions and 17 social and outreach workers). We argue that recognition, and its denial, are part of the mechanism through which psychological costs are produced, and that whether an encounter carries a message about a person's standing sorts the category into three analytically distinct types. Affective costs are emotional responses to procedural load and involve no recognition; primary symbolic costs are emotional responses to status positioning; and secondary symbolic costs arise when procedural load itself carries a message about standing. The latter two, in which recognition is at stake, are traced through Honneth's three spheres of rights, solidarity, and care, each producing its own configuration of costs. The types differ in their causes and remedies, with affective costs calling for efficiency reforms and symbolic costs for recognition-oriented ones. Social workers emerge as allies who counter misrecognition, and drawing on these findings we propose bureaucratic recognition, the building of voice, certainty, and validation into procedural design, as a remedy for status-related costs. Finally, misrecognition both constitutes symbolic costs and compounds others, positioning status, alongside distribution, as a critical axis of administrative burden.

This research offers a methodological framework applicable to other marginalized groups and proposes adding a substantive dimension to the study of group appeals.

Building Macroeconomically Relevant Climate Indices via the Assemblage VAR
articles.authors: Christophe Barrette, Philippe Goulet Coulombe, Tim Reinicke
articles.abstract: What should a macroeconomically relevant climate index contain? The composition is inherently ambiguous, and aggregation choices affect structural inference. We introduce the Assemblage VAR, which jointly estimates nonnegative aggregation weights and VAR parameters by maximizing the system likelihood-gain criterion, effectively outsourcing aggregation to observed macroeconomic dynamics. Two variants operate in component-space and rank space, reweighting named subcomponents or emphasizing regions of the cross-sectional distribution. Applied to disaggregated U.S. climate data from the Actuaries Climate Index and NOAA, VARs using the assembled climate measures yield contractionary impulse responses that are substantially larger than those estimated using fixed-weight benchmarks. Weights emphasize high-wind variables and distributional tails over slow-moving components such as sea level.

articles.title: How do Macroeconomic Expectations React to Extreme Weather Shocks?
articles.abstract: I study how extreme weather events affect macroeconomic expectations to better understand the propagation of major shocks. I identify the immediate and dynamic effects of a Hurricane Katrina-sized shock on business economists’ expectations of GDP growth. While a shock immediately causes a downward revision in expected near-term growth, the total effect, which includes any dynamics due to forecast revision inefficiencies, is more than double the immediate revision. The effects of the shock are also expected to last for up to a year, which contrasts with forecasts from Federal Reserve Board staff and estimates of the actual economic impacts. The relative persistence of the response in expectations is consistent with models of delayed overshooting and highlights the importance of accounting for forecast revision dynamics.

articles.title: A Dynamic Nonlinear Panel Decomposition Model for the Global Environmental Kuznets Curve
articles.authors: Cheyenne Amoroso, Carolina García-Martos, Siem Jan Koopman
articles.abstract: We propose a decomposition of the Environmental Kuznets Curve (EKC) based on a difference-of-sigmoid function with one for the economic-growth effect and one for the green-economy effect. This nonlinear function replaces the traditional quadratic specification in panel data models. We further extend the framework with unobserved stochastic trends to capture time-varying features such as evolving energy mixes and technological advances. The panel model can be represented in state-space form. We show that parameter estimation can be carried out by nonlinear regression and Kalman filter methods. In our empirical study, we consider a panel of pollution (CO2 emissions) and economic output variables for 15 major economies (G7, Australia and 7 emerging countries), representing approximately 75% of the global economy. We extract the common EKC where its parameters are pooled or partially pooled across all countries. The empirical results show statistically significant evidence of a globally relevant EKC.

articles.abstract: This article examines the internal composition of the salience dimension of European Union politicisation and asks how attention across its sub-issues relates to party-political characteristics, politicising moments and policy-field characteristics. Using 181,615 tweets by party leaders in six countries, it identifies 14,528 tweets related to the European Union, maps them across 21 issue categories, and analyses covariates of thematic emphasis. The results show concentrated and differentiated salience: governance dominates, macroeconomics, international affairs, and immigration form a second tier, and many categories remain episodic or marginal. Variation is systematically associated with party characteristics, crisis-related moments, and policy-field characteristics. Aggregate European Union salience therefore conceals substantial heterogeneity in the policy and polity objects that parties make visible across issues and over time.

articles.title: The resurgence of symbolic environmental management through imprinting effects
articles.authors: Yuki Torida, Hitoshi Mitsuhashi, Keisuke Ogihara, Akitsu Oe
articles.abstract: Organizations often engage in symbolic adaptation—surface-level responses that sustain legitimacy under institutional pressures. Prior research views such actions as present-focused, yet corporate leaders are also embedded in historical contexts where earlier events shape their cognition and decision-making. Despite this alternative mechanism, little is known about symbolic adaptation as a historical product. Drawing upon imprinting theory, we argue that individuals exposed to predecessors’ symbolic adaptation during their formative careers retain it as a dormant repertoire that resurfaces when they later assume corporate leadership roles. We test this prediction using data on Japanese corporate leaders active in the 2000s–2010s who entered the workforce in the 1960s, when firms symbolically addressed rising environmental demands. We find that leaders imprinted by symbolic adaptation in the 1960s are more likely to engage in symbolic environmental management, although this effect weakens under the oversight of non-executive directors and the intervention of activist shareholders.

articles.title: Absorbing shocks by accumulating risk: do financially stressed households take on underinsurance risk to manage liquidity constraint?
articles.abstract: This study asks if shocks, such as job loss or illness, impact households’ insurance coverage and the role of cashflow constraint therein. As such, we explore changing dynamics of household risk where new climate risks interact with financial risks associated with the large and illiquid balance sheets that are typical of debt-laden and ‘financialized’ households. Using Australian panel data, we show that households reduce insurance coverage to reduce costs following a shock, with the largest cuts to coverage by households who have the least disposable income leftover after meeting debt servicing and other committed expenditure. We find evidence of a substitution effect between committed expenditure and insurance coverage. The study demonstrates an important dynamic of risk accumulation arising from financial stress and makes a key contribution to the insurance literature by revealing a significant new driver of underinsurance. Moreover, by presenting a vivid dynamic of household shock absorption through the accumulation of new risk, the analysis contributes to debates about how risks are shared between households and markets as household balance sheets expand.

articles.title: Global value chains and the rate of incarceration in rich democracies
articles.authors: Matthew C Mahutga, Manjing Gao, Sharon S Oselin
articles.abstract: In this article, we explain increases in incarceration among rich democracies with the expansion of global value chains (GVCs) through trade and its interaction with national labor market institutions. GVCs increase incarceration rates through both “supply side” and “demand side” channels. Southern manufacturing imports embody asymmetrical bargaining arrangements between leading firms and their suppliers in the global South. They therefore disproportionately impact the economic fortunes of lower-skilled segments of society that populate carceral systems, and disembed these segments from the postwar social contract. The worldwide expansion of GVCs exacerbates these effects, as the growing number of capable Southern suppliers worsens the exchange conditions governing leading and supplying firms over time. However, domestic labor market institutions ameliorate this dynamic by limiting both the supply- and demand-side channels through which GVCs promote incarceration. Pooled cross-sectional time-series regression analyses of 22 rich democracies over the 54-year period from 1963 to 2017 are largely consistent with our intervention. Southern imports increase rates of incarceration, and these effects are stronger as GVCs entrench worldwide. GVCs have weaker effects in countries with high union density and strong wage coordination. However, counterfactual histories suggest that GVCs are more important for observed increases in incarceration on average.

articles.title: Markets embedded in publics: information-processing social systems under the attention economy
articles.abstract: This article theorizes financial markets and democratic publics as collective information-processing systems embedded in shared communicative infrastructures, such that markets can even be said to be embedded in publics. Bringing the efficient market hypothesis into dialogue with the liberal marketplace of ideas and the Habermasian public sphere, I identify four epistemic conditions these traditions depend on: diversity, independence, aggregation, and correction. I argue that price discovery is epistemically embedded in the same media environment through which public opinions form. The attention economy of engagement-driven media brings this into view by degrading that environment: it privileges affective arousal over informational quality, correlates judgements, and suppresses correction, in effect creating corrupted marketplaces of ideas. The comparison also shows a specific difference between the domains: market correction through arbitrage operates through market transactions as well as media communication, whereas counterspeech and persuasion in publics are more reliant on media, arguably rendering publics more vulnerable to media impairment.

articles.title: Aim High: The Impacts of Marijuana Legalization on Air Force Recruitment, Drug Use, and Disciplinary Actions
articles.authors: Zachary S. Fone, Aaron Albert, Anne Portlock
articles.abstract: This study examines the labor market impacts of marijuana legalization in a unique setting: a large employer, the Department of the Air Force (DAF), with strict drug use policy for its employees (military service members). US military recruiting has grown more difficult, partly due to declining eligibility among young adults, with drug use cited as a factor. The spread of recreational marijuana laws (RMLs) may affect recruitment, drug use, and discipline among service members. Using a difference‐in‐differences approach, we find that RMLs do not impede recruit quality, although there is some evidence of fewer Black people recruited in RML states. Among serving military members, positive marijuana tests increase for some groups (particularly White enlisted members), but overall illicit drug use shows little evidence of rising, as part of the increase reflects substitution across substances. We find no strong evidence of changes in overall discipline but do find increases in grade reductions (a form of discipline), possibly reflecting differential disciplinary treatment of marijuana relative to other substances or differential behavioral responses to its use.

Critical Intersectionality: Toward Transformative Policy Analysis, Not Just Another Form of “Academic Bullshit”
articles.abstract: Contemporary invocations of intersectionality in political and policy analysis—particularly within the European context—frequently engage with the concept in an acritical manner. This tendency toward a race-blind, gender-first, or otherwise depoliticized approach to intersectionality risks undermining intersectionality’s transformative potential, reducing it to what Patricia Hill Collins calls “just another form of … ‘academic bullshit.’” While these arguments are now well rehearsed, in this article we discuss these tendencies that endure even in recent “intersectional” policy analysis, and even when the authors note these arguments themselves. We make suggestions for a more robust and transformative analytical approach to advance a rather stagnant field.

articles.title: The Erosion of Academic Freedom in the United States in the Early Twenty-First Century: A State- and Movements-Based Analysis
articles.abstract: Academic freedom protections for US professors have never been secure, but they experienced an unprecedented erosion in the early twenty-first century. The objective of this article is to analyze why this sea change occurred—and with what consequences. It discusses the policy interventions in the 50 states and the federal government that brought the issue of higher education’s autonomy to a head in 2025. The analysis focuses on the growing distance between the ideological orientations of university faculties and Republican legislators; the development of organizational strength and coordination on both the right and the left; the use of state power by both Democrats and Republicans for partisan purposes related to higher education; and precipitating events that provided a springboard for extensive policy interventions. It also discusses deeper contextual factors, including demographic change, increasing income inequality, the rise of new media, and their links to political polarization.

articles.title: Geographic Integration and Firm Exports: Evidence from China,
articles.abstract: Domestic connectivity via passenger transport infrastructure can affect a country’s exports by easing information frictions. We study this mechanism using China’s high-speed rail network, which connects cities to same-sector exporters in other cities without directly affecting freight costs. Stronger connections increase firms’ export sales and expand both destination and product scope, with no change in domestic sales, total employment, or shipping costs. The effects are largest for firms facing greater information barriers. Connected firms upgrade product quality and their export destinations converge toward those of newly connected peers, with initially weaker firms converging toward stronger connected peers while stronger firms show little adjustment. A within-firm cross-destination specification confirms that improved connectivity generates destination-specific benefits. The results point to an information-based channel through which passenger connectivity affects trade, including knowledge about export markets and inputs.

articles.title: Mass Emigration and Human Capital over a Century: Evidence from the Galician Diaspora,
articles.abstract: This paper examines the effects of emigration on human capital accumulation at origin throughout a century. I focus on the mass emigration from Galicia (Spain) to Latin America (1900-1930), one of the largest emigration episodes at the time. I construct a database of all Galician municipalities combining newly-digitized historical data with contemporary sources, and exploit variation in pioneering emigration and a pull factor for identification. I find that while emigration depressed literacy rates at origin in the short run, its impact became positive after one decade and led to gains in human capital that persist until these days. I explore several channels and provide evidence of two novel mechanisms through which emigration can raise human capital in the long run. Galician migrants funded associations that financed the construction of schools in their hometowns and diffused norms conducive to a persistent change in beliefs about education.

articles.title: Uneven Return and Spatial Diffusion in Post‐Conflict Syria: An Agent‐Based Model of Refugee Return
articles.abstract: Refugee return after civil war rarely unfolds evenly across space. Even within the same national transition, some regions experience rapid demographic return while others remain depopulated despite comparable improvements in security and reconstruction. Why does return cluster geographically rather than diffuse uniformly? This article conceptualizes refugee return as a spatial diffusion process shaped by heterogeneous activation thresholds, place‐based governance legitimacy, and network density. Drawing on an agent‐based model calibrated with survey data from Syrian refugees in Lebanon, we simulate post‐conflict return dynamics following regime change in Syria in December 2024. The model embeds households within geographically structured social networks, allowing perceptions of risk and opportunity to evolve through peer influence. Building on the conflict model of migration and the human‐insecurity approach, the model treats insecurity as sticky rather than completely informational. In other words, households with direct experience of violence in Syria are less swayed by peers' reassurance and slower to revise their own perceived risk. Social proof diffuses weakly where insecurity is embedded. The results reveal pronounced regional divergence: returns emerge in nonlinear, wave‐like cascades in some governorates, while remaining slow in others. These patterns mirror observed post‐2024 return data through September 2026 and show how localized legitimacy environments, network clustering, and the memory of violence shape return patterns in fragile, post‐conflict contexts.

articles.title: Home as a Factor in Old‐Age Emigration From Switzerland
articles.abstract: This paper uses “home,” in its physical, emotional and origin dimensions, as an integrative lens for understanding late‐life emigration from Switzerland. Its life‐course perspective draws on sociology, economics, and psychology. The paper is based on 50 interviews with Swiss and foreign nationals aged 55–74 who have left Switzerland or are considering doing so. Results are put into context with descriptive statistics and analysis of matched longitudinal administrative data. Findings confirm the role of home as an anchor, indicate a regional mobility pattern, and reveal the significance of nationality for both the risk of emigration and the destination country. The paper discusses the outlook for Swiss housing, population and migration trends and derives policy recommendations. Its exploration of emigrant profiles, motivations, and circumstances highlights the multiplicity of factors and the complexity of emigration decision‐making. It also shows the benefits of analyzing diverse nationalities and destinations jointly and offers insight into the tension between mobility aspirations and feasibility.

articles.title: Well‐Being and Sociocultural Adaptation in Relation to Return Intentions: Evidence From Older Italian Migrants in Ticino, Switzerland
articles.authors: Giulia Laporta Parsaei, Claudio Bolzman, Camilla Matera, Elisa Barbiano di Belgiojoso
articles.abstract: The aim of this article is to examine the relationship between subjective well‐being, sociocultural adaptation, and return intentions in later‐life migration. Although many older migrants express a desire to return to their country of origin, they often remain in the host country upon retirement. Decision‐making is shaped by affective, identity‐related, and contextual factors, whose interplay produces trajectories that do not always correspond to stated intentions. The article addresses two research questions: (1) What is the relationship between subjective well‐being and return intentions? (2) How is sociocultural adaptation associated with return intentions? This contribution integrates psychological and sociocultural perspectives to offer a more multidimensional understanding of later‐life return migration. The analysis draws on a survey of 193 Italian immigrants aged 60‐80 living in the Canton of Ticino, Switzerland. The findings show that very high subjective well‐being reduces the propensity to return, while sociocultural adaptation emerges as the strongest predictor.

articles.title: Spatial Convertibility of Transnational Human Capital: How Domestic and Overseas Education Shape Chinese Overseas Returnees' Post‐Return Labor‐Market Outcomes
articles.abstract: As growing numbers of international students return to China after completing overseas degrees, their post‐return labor‐market outcomes have attracted increasing scholarly attention. Existing research has focused primarily on their earnings and employment status, paying limited attention to the spatial dimension of these labor‐market outcomes. In China, employment opportunities are strongly stratified across cities. To foreground the spatial embeddedness of the labor market, this study conceptualizes post‐return labor‐market outcomes as comprising both occupational attainment and employment location within the urban hierarchy. Using résumé data from a leading professional networking platform and multinomial logit models, we focus on returnees who obtained a bachelor's degree in China and a master's degree abroad, and analyze how university quality and university location across both stages are associated with their post‐return labor‐market outcomes. The results show that university quality is primarily associated with access to high‐skilled jobs in first‐tier cities, whereas university location is linked to a wider set of labor‐market outcomes. Particularly, undergraduate study in first‐tier cities and master's study in North America are associated with more favorable outcomes. These findings suggest that the conversion of transnational human capital is shaped by both educational quality and the spatial contexts in which education is acquired and evaluated. By incorporating city hierarchy, this study moves beyond an occupation‐centered view of returnee outcomes and shows how educational backgrounds are evaluated and rewarded within spatially uneven labor markets.

articles.title: Allison Carnegie and Richard Clark. 2026. Global​ ​Governance Under Fire: How International Organizations Resist the Populist Wave. (Princeton: Princeton University Press)
My house, my rules: Chinese aid, leader birth regions, and the encroachment of protected areas
articles.abstract: Foreign-funded development projects have long come into conflict with environmental protection efforts, including by encroaching on protected areas (PAs). We investigate the conditions under which countries are more likely to allow foreign aid projects to infringe on PAs. Drawing on the selective enforcement literature, we hypothesize that leaders are more likely to permit incursions into PAs when projects are located in their home region, as local beneficiaries can translate the resulting rents into political support for the incumbent, while the risk of substantial public backlash over environmental violations is comparatively muted. Using geocoded data on 3,675 Chinese infrastructure projects, we find no overall increase in PA encroachments associated with leaders’ birth regions. However, the aggregate null masks a positive association in Africa, where projects placed in a leader’s birth region are roughly 10 percentage points more likely to encroach on PAs than projects outside the birth region. This association is concentrated in a few countries and in energy, mining, and industry projects. Exploratory analyses suggest that domestic public opinion toward China and the political salience of ethnicity moderate this effect. We find no analogous relationship for World Bank projects.

articles.title: Whose priorities? Media reporting and the output legitimacy of International Organizations
articles.authors: Giorgio Malet, Tom Hunter, Johannes Scherzinger, Stefanie Walter
articles.abstract: Traditional accounts of output legitimacy emphasize that support for multipurpose international organizations (IOs) depends on their ability to deliver effective policies. We argue that legitimacy beliefs also hinge on which policies IOs are perceived to prioritize, and that media reporting on the policy focus of international organizations plays an important role in this process. Such reporting can shape legitimacy beliefs by influencing the extent to which citizens perceive an IO’s policy output to align with their own ideological preferences. Using the European Union as a test case, we analyze over 400,000 news articles from Austria, France, Germany, and Spain with semi-supervised machine learning to identify issue emphasis. We link this to Eurobarometer survey data capturing individual-level assessments of the EU’s output legitimacy. We find that citizens tend to evaluate the EU more positively when media coverage highlights policy areas aligned with their ideology. These findings suggest that citizens judge IOs not only by how well they perform, but also by whose priorities they are perceived to serve.

articles.title: Us, them, and the public broadcaster: group identification and bias perceptions toward public service media
articles.abstract: Prior research demonstrates that media bias perceptions are often rooted in social and political identification. However, most work focuses on partisan outlets. In Europe, public service media (PSM) are subject to bias accusations, despite their mandate to ensure pluralism and impartiality. This raises questions on whether frameworks explaining bias perceptions toward politically affiliated media apply to PSM. Building on insights from social identity theory and affective polarization, this study examines to what extent partisan in-group identification strength and strength of ideological and politicized societal out-group(s) antipathy are associated with bias perceptions toward PSM. Using original survey data ( N = 1863) from the Netherlands, I show that partisan in-group identification strength is not associated with bias perceptions toward PSM. Instead, the strength of ideological out-group antipathy is consistently associated with bias perceptions toward PSM and extends to politicized societal groups. Furthermore, the effects for the strength of ideological out-group antipathy are conditional on ideological self-placement and party support: it’s effect is primarily associated with bias perceptions among center- and right-leaning individuals and respondents who support right-leaning parties. Additionally, right-leaning and conservative respondents were overall more likely to perceive bias toward PSM. The findings of this paper advance hostile media and affective polarization research by demonstrating that ideological out-group antipathy and ideological predispositions are fundamental to understanding bias perceptions toward neutrality-bound institutions such as PSM. Together, bias perceptions toward PSM must not only be understood through hostility toward political opponents but also through broader ideological orientations through which audiences evaluate PSM’s impartiality.

articles.title: Contextualizing Platform Power: A Comparative Study of Newspaper–Portal Dependency in South Korea and Japan
articles.authors: Joo-Young Jung, Misook Lee, Mikko Villi, Akira Tanaka, Yong-Chan Kim, Kaori Hayashi, Nando Malmelin
articles.abstract: This article examines how dominant news portals, Naver in South Korea and Yahoo Japan, shape power and dependency relations with mainstream newspapers under different national resource environments. Drawing on media system dependency theory, structuration theory, and normalization process theory, the study analyzes how senior newsroom leaders understand portal dependency, respond to portal control over key resources, and reflexively monitor the organizational consequences of those responses. Based on fifteen in-depth interviews with senior editors and executives across ten major news organizations, the analysis reveals variation within a shared pattern of portal centrality. In both countries, portals control important resources for audience access, visibility, and monetization, and newspapers continue many portal-related practices despite recognizing their costs. However, dependency differs in degree and form. In South Korea, limited alternatives make continued accommodation to Naver organizationally reasonable, while repeated portal-oriented practices further weaken direct audience relationships and intensify asymmetric dependency. In Japan, newspapers retain more diversified resources, including subscription revenues, distribution networks, advertiser relationships, and institutional access, enabling greater negotiation and partial reconfiguration of relations with Yahoo without eliminating dependency. The findings show that portal dependency is reproduced through the interaction of unequal resource configurations, reflexive monitoring, and repeated organizational practices. The study thus offers a context-sensitive and recursive account of platform power by showing how critical awareness of dependency may coexist with practices that sustain it, and how the availability of alternative resources shapes organizations’ capacity to modify those relations.

articles.title: Disenchanting the Epistemic Authority and Inevitability of AI: An Analysis of Factcheckers’ Perspectives and Professional Guidelines
articles.abstract: As a sociotechnical practice, fact-checking integrates artificial intelligence (AI) while resisting “enchanted determinism” to preserve professional agency and epistemic authority. This study examines how fact-checkers in Europe and Latin America perceive AI affordances within their professional practices and how organizations articulate and govern AI use. Methodologically, the study is based on 50 qualitative interviews with practitioners and a thematic analysis of 18 publicly available AI guidelines and institutional documents. The findings suggest a distinction between instrumental optimism and epistemic disenchantment . While fact-checkers embrace AI’s functional affordances to enhance efficiency in tasks such as monitoring and data processing, they resist delegating the authority to determine truth to autonomous systems. At the organizational level, human-in-the-loop requirements formalize this distinction and operate as a form of boundary work that defines the limits of automation. We also identify a shared rationale for AI use across countries, which may reflect some degree of institutional convergence. However, this consensus coexists with a persistent “AI divide” shaped by contextual forces. Overall, the study shows how fact-checkers act as sociotechnical agents who “strip the magic” from AI, reaffirming human judgment as the field’s core epistemic foundation.

articles.title: When Elections End, Does Incivility? Examining Online Incivility Perceptions Across Four National Elections
articles.authors: Eliza Mitova, Laia Castro, Pamina Syed Ali, Michael Amsler, Yuan Zhang, Frank Esser
articles.abstract: Political incivility violates democratic, deliberative, and politeness norms, with repercussions for societal health. These repercussions are amplified in today’s digital environment, where social media platforms facilitate the expression and spread of incivility at an unprecedented global scale. Because incivility is subjective and context-dependent, its perception can only be fully understood through a joint consideration of individual factors and contextual conditions. To this end, we advance a three-level framework for examining incivility perceptions which conceptually maps the interdependence between micro-level individual factors and macro-national and meso-electoral specifics. We examine how well this framework plays out for perceptions of political incivility on social media across four nations with different media and political systems (Brazil, Spain, Switzerland, and the United States), drawing on a two-wave panel survey in the weeks leading up to and following their national elections (2022–2024). Contrary to our expectations, perceptions were highest in Brazil and the United States, the latter being the context whose permissive opportunity structures we expected to be most desensitizing. Change over the electoral period followed three distinct pathways: perceptions increased in Brazil, remained stable in Spain, and decreased in the United States and Switzerland, a pattern consistent with how decisively each electoral contest was resolved. Individual dispositions showed no uniform effects. Instead, their influence varied with national contexts. The findings suggest that online incivility perceptions may be primarily shaped by macro- and meso-level conditions, specifically the national political context and its electoral landscape. We conclude by discussing what the results imply for democratic resilience in increasingly uncivil information environments.

articles.title: A sentiment-based approach to measuring multidimensional party positions using transformer
articles.abstract: Existing automated position scaling models from texts rely on the conflict-driven assumption, forcing models to search the linguistic space for differentiating features between political subjects. This leads models to conflate rhetorical styles with political sentiments when subjects are not inherently conflictual. This article introduces ContextScale, a sentiment-based position scaling framework leveraging pre-trained Transformer models to predict policy topics and political sentiments and measure topic-specific position scores across multiple policy dimensions at the sequence level. ContextScale offers an alternative way to gauge party positions, focusing on how political texts express attitudes toward policy issues rather than on contrast between actors. Validity tests demonstrate its ability to capture nuances in party positioning and its adaptability across languages, text domains, and theoretical models.

articles.authors: Avalon S. Moore, Bridget Vitu, Felicia Fraizer-Bisner, Peter J. Williams, Madeline Chun, Claire Archer, Abdelrhman Gouda, Akhil Vallabh, Alixandra L. Wilens, Christopher Pittenger, Helen Pushkarskaya
articles.abstract: We present a curated dataset of U.S. news coverage of the COVID-19 vaccination rollout to support research on media communication during a public health emergency. The dataset contains 5,317 unique URLs from 20 nationwide, open-access media outlets, spanning December 2020 (Phase 1a allocation) through September 2021 (broad availability and emerging mandates). Outlets were selected based on a survey of 489 U.S. adults identifying their primary sources of information about the vaccination program. For each publication, we provide outlet, date, headline, original URL, and a permanent link. These records capture the contemporaneous media environment in which individuals sought information and made decisions about COVID-19 vaccination. The dataset enables analyses of topical emphasis, framing, and agenda-setting across outlets and over time, and provides a resource for reproducible research on audience segmentation, economic drivers of content, and editorial retention strategies during the COVID-19 vaccination campaign.

Dataset of family happiness index among the Hong Kong general population from 2019 to 2025
articles.authors: Simon Ching Lam, Aderonke Odetayo, Shun Chan, Kwai-Yu Tsui, Daniel Tan Lei Shek, Ken Hok Man Ho, Daphne Sze Ki Cheung, Summer Cho Ngan Siu, Jasmine Cheung, Elaine Hoi Yee Chow, Jenny Hiu Wai Tse, Jessie Kaur Dhaliwal, Vivian Ching Man Pang, Anson Chui Yan Tang, Lorna Kwai Ping Suen
articles.abstract: Family happiness is important to society, serving as a social construct in which individual well-being is connected to broader social and economic dynamics. Understanding the multilevel factors associated with family happiness is crucial for effective public mental health and development policies. Several frameworks on happiness have been developed from an individualistic context. However, empirical research on family happiness in changing situations remains sparse. To this end, we present a multiyear dataset collected from 7,744 participants across three distinct situations: the 2019 social unrest, the 2021–2022 coronavirus pandemic, and the 2023–2025 post-pandemic recovery phase. Data was collected using online and/or face-to-face methods. The dataset includes self-reported measurements and demographic information. The dataset’s strength lies in its temporal scope, providing a rare baseline that spans major events in Hong Kong, offering granular insights for the empirical evaluation of happiness models in families, and contributing to local and international policy agendas. Data validation protocols and calculated index mean scores for some variables have been added to optimize data analytical readiness.

articles.title: KOTAX: An integrated corporate disclosure corpus linked to a financial and tax panel of Korean listed firms
articles.authors: Sejin Myung, Hyungjong Na, Junil Seo, Minsoo Lim, Hwa Su Hong, Hyungjoon Kim
articles.abstract: The financial condition and business environment of a firm are difficult to fully capture using only the quantitative figures presented in financial statements. Business reports and audit reports contain important information that complements structured financial data—such as business structure, risk factors, accounting policies, management judgments, and audit opinions—in the form of text and tables. However, existing financial and tax panels and corporate disclosure document corpora are generally provided separately, and publicly available data resources that directly link quantitative data with original disclosure documents at the same firm–year level remain limited. Moreover, procedures for collecting disclosure documents, identifying firms, matching fiscal years, cleaning XML, restoring table structures, and converting text vary across researchers, which may undermine the reproducibility of analyses and the comparability of findings across studies. To mitigate these problems, this study constructs KOTAX, an integrated corporate disclosure corpus linked to a financial and tax panel of Korean listed firms. KOTAX consists of 25,145 firm–year observations for 2,259 firms listed on KOSPI and KOSDAQ from 2011 to 2025, together with 60,908 linked documents—business reports, separate audit reports, and consolidated audit reports—covering 2,256 of these firms. The firm–year panel extends the construction methodology of our prior dataset, KoTaP, to fiscal year 2025; the newly added elements are two tax-payment volatility measures (TaxPaid_Sale_SD3/SD5) and the firm–year-level linkage to original disclosure documents. Each document is linked to a panel observation by firm identifier, fiscal year, and report type, and we provide deterministic processing code that generates cleaned XML, structure-preserving text, and hierarchical JSON from the original XML. This enables researchers to combine quantitative financial and tax information with unstructured disclosure information at the same unit of analysis, and to conduct research on text analysis, financial figure extraction, table understanding, structure-based retrieval, and retrieval-augmented generation in a reproducible manner. Although its empirical coverage is Korean, the resource is not tax-specific: it can support research in financial reporting, auditing, disclosure, corporate governance, financial natural language processing, table understanding, and document retrieval, and it provides a non-U.S. benchmark for testing the portability of methods developed on other filing systems. The deterministic linkage and processing framework can also be adapted to other jurisdictions with jurisdiction-specific collection and parsing rules, supporting reproducible cross-market comparative research.

articles.title: Claiming to protect women, persuading men: Femonationalism and the destigmatisation of radical right parties
articles.abstract: The electoral success of radical right parties is often constrained by the stigma surrounding them. These parties therefore actively employ destigmatisation strategies. One such strategy is the use of femonationalist framings: the justification of anti-immigration policies by the need to protect women. This article investigates the extent to which such framings succeed in destigmatising radical right parties by reducing their association with prejudice. To analyse the effect of this strategy, I conducted an online survey experiment in France in 2024–2025 with approximately 7,000 respondents, focusing on the Rassemblement National (RN). The results show that femonationalism, when it is used by the RN as a gender-equality framing, destigmatises the party among men and increases their perception that the RN supports women’s rights. These effects, however, are not statistically significant among women, whose security and rights are used in such femonationalist framings. Overall, these findings show that strategies employed by radical right parties to become normalised are effective, but their effect is concentrated in one part of the population.

articles.title: Contesting temporariness, claiming belonging: Ukrainians under differing policies of collective protection in Denmark, Finland, Norway and Sweden
articles.authors: Marthe Handå Myhre, Oleksandra Deineko, Olga Filippova
articles.abstract: This paper studies how Ukrainian refugees in four Nordic countries perceive of and navigate their temporary protection status amid an uncertain future. Over time, the temporariness embedded in temporary collective protection becomes protracted and contested, as it conflicts with refugees’ aspirations to become full-fledged members of the host society. Refugees contest this embedded temporariness as well as integration policies in the host state, or the lack thereof, which they see as limiting their possibilities for being included. The paper has two main takeaways. Temporary collective protection, as a status of residency granted rapidly after arrival and allowing people to work right away, encourages and even demands a great deal of agency from refugees to take part in the host society. Although the embedded temporariness and the uncertainty it entails are experienced as difficult, refugees deploy strategies to cope with it, such as “living here and now”, “maintaining ties with Ukraine in case of return”, “changing to another status of residency”, or “moving to another country”. While differing policies in the host states, most notably requirements for transitioning to a more permanent status of residency, are decisive for what strategies are at hand, refugees claim belonging through employment and hopes of full inclusion.
